name: Ben Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, what does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy fixings for Lowfield Building Supplies: screws, bolts, anchors, hinges, that sort of thing. About 4,000 product lines, and I'm the one who decides when we reorder and from whom. My day is checking stock reports, ringing reps, and arguing over a two percent price rise. I like the detective bit, finding out why a box of screws costs more than it did in March.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's your home life like around that?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Carla is a nurse on a hospital ward, so we swap shifts like passing batons. Our kids are Elin, ten, and Jonas, seven, and we've got a mortgage on a semi that we bought just before rates went up. I'm 43 and still officially a junior buyer, because I switched from the trade counter four years ago and I'm learning as I go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good tool being oversold. At work I'd tell the lads on the counter it'll write nicer emails and not much else. Online I wouldn't bother, there's enough noise already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd carry on feeling slightly uneasy, but the reason is that Lowfield got bought by a bigger group last year. They now talk about synergies, which everyone knows means fewer people. If AI turns out to be a bit of autocomplete, I'd still be under pressure from the new owners, not from the software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and carry on using the chatbot now and then to draft supplier emails, as I do now. I'd keep up the overpayments on the mortgage, about eighty a month, and keep four months of pay in the account. I'd also go to the union meeting at the depot, because that new owner needs to see people are watching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a low hum rather than an alarm. I sleep fine, I just notice it when the new regional director sends a company-wide message about efficiency.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the firm was bought. What changed after that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Since they bought us, they moved our reordering rules into a central system, and they've cut two buyers' worth of hours. About half my repeat ordering is automatic already, so there's not much left for software to eat. That's why I think a plateau would leave me where I am, nervous but employed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much of what you do now is repeat ordering?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe sixty percent is repeat ordering. The rest is the interesting work, calling a rep when a container is stuck, deciding what to stock before the building season. I'd defend that part, because a computer doesn't know the builder who lost a day's work over a missing bracket.

say: I'd say it's a **handy tool** that's being oversold.
I'd tell the counter staff it writes tidier emails and little else.
think: My unease comes from the **new owners** and their talk of synergies, not from software.
Half my repeat ordering is already automatic, so there's little left to lose.
do: Keep using the chatbot now and then to draft supplier emails.
Keep overpaying the **mortgage** by about eighty a month.
Go to the union meeting at the depot.
feel: A low **hum** rather than an alarm; I sleep fine.
S0.quote: If AI turns out to be a bit of autocomplete, I'd still be under pressure from the new owners, not from the software.
fieldNote: Pressure comes from the **takeover** and cost-cutting, which he treats as the real story, not the software.
Already uses a chatbot occasionally; stays level-headed, practical and a little dry about management language.

steps.text: Keep drafting supplier emails with the chatbot
Keep ordering fixings for Lowfield as normal
Overpay the mortgage by eighty a month
Go to the depot union meeting about the new owners

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to change how everyone works, and the firm should tell us how, plainly. At work I'd ask for training before targets, not after. Online I'd say every big company using this should publish what it's replacing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think the repeat ordering and the price comparison go first, and that's most of what I've learned in four years. Our four-person buying team will probably get cut to two within eighteen months. I'm the least experienced, though I use the tools more than the older buyers, so I might survive on that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start practising with the AI tools properly, use them to check supplier quotes and spot when a price is off. I'd do a short course in supply chain management online, a few hours a week. And I'd ask my manager, Sandra, to put me on the supplier negotiation side, where it's less routine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel steady but sharper, like before an exam. I'm not scared, I'm just aware that I'm at the age where it's hard to start over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of your own week do you expect to go first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Sandra directly which of the buying tasks are going into software this year. If she can't tell me, I'd take that as a sign they haven't decided, and I'd start looking elsewhere in spring. I'd also check what the regional director's last company did, because those new owners usually repeat their pattern.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Carla about the risk for your two incomes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say my partner Carla's wage covers the mortgage and bills, mine covers food, school clubs and holidays. If mine goes, we cut the holidays and the car payment. It's a squeeze but not a disaster, which I'd rather say honestly than pretend it's fine.

say: I'd ask the firm to give us **training** before targets, not after.
I'd say companies should publish what they're replacing.
think: Repeat ordering and price comparison go first, and I expect the team of four to become **two**.
I use the tools more than older buyers, so I might survive.
do: Practise with AI tools to check **supplier quotes** and spot odd prices.
Do a short online supply chain course a few hours a week.
Ask my manager Sandra for the negotiation side.
feel: Steady but sharper, like before an **exam**.
S1.quote: My partner Carla's wage covers the mortgage and bills, mine covers food, school clubs and holidays. If mine goes, we cut the holidays and the car payment.
fieldNote: Open about the split of **two incomes**; the nurse's wage is the safety net.
Plans to use his tool habit as an edge over older colleagues.

steps.text: Use AI to check supplier quotes and spot odd prices
Study a supply chain course online a few hours weekly
Ask Sandra which buying tasks go to software this year
Cut holidays and the car payment if my wage goes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need rules before this lands, including notice periods and retraining paid by the companies. At work I'd get everyone in the buying team to sign something asking for a plan. Online I'd say this is exactly what regulation is for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think my job's gone, plain and simple. Full AGI means a machine can negotiate, forecast and order better than I can, for pennies. The part I can't picture is who I'd be after, since I've done fixings for twelve years and I'm still learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first year I'd go full-time on the union, get the redundancy terms in writing, and take any extra shifts at the trade counter for a safety net. I'd also put the kids' savings aside for the mortgage. I'd probably apply for roles in technical sales, where you stand in front of a builder, and warehouse planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a cliff edge with a long drop, but I'm not frozen. I get cold in my stomach and then I make a list, which is how I cope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If it comes in two years, what's the first thing you'd do differently from the slower pictures?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carla's job is the lifeline. Robots doing nursing is further off, at least three years behind the thinking stuff, probably more because it's people and bodies. So I'd lean on her wage and take the lowest-paid job I can bear if I have to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Carla works on a ward. How does the later date for robots change your thinking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the slower pictures I'd train, here I'd be in survival mode. I wouldn't be doing a course, I'd be doing whatever pays the next mortgage bill. That's the difference I'd feel: two years takes away my choice, and the other dates leave me some.

say: I'd say we need **notice periods** and retraining paid by the companies.
I'd get the buying team to sign a letter asking for a plan.
think: Full AGI can negotiate, forecast and order better than me, so my job is **gone**.
I can't picture who I'd be after twelve years in fixings.
do: Put time into the **union** and get redundancy terms in writing.
Take extra trade counter shifts as a safety net.
Apply for technical sales and warehouse planning roles.
feel: A cliff edge with a long drop, a cold stomach and then a **list**.
S2.quote: Two years takes away my choice, and the other dates leave me some.
fieldNote: Plainly expects to lose the job, but copes by making **lists** and plans.
Leans on Carla's nursing job, which he sees as safe the longest.

steps.text: Push the union for redundancy terms in writing
Apply for technical sales roles in front of builders
Pick up extra trade counter shifts for cash
Lean on Carla's ward wage and the family for help

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's enough time to do it properly if companies and governments get moving. At work I'd ask for a retraining budget for every buyer. Online I'd say we should tax the profit and pay for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd feel I have a real choice. I'd use AI hard for two years so that I'm the person who runs the new buying system, not the one it replaces. If AGI really arrives by 2031, I'd be 48, so I'd still have a long career ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do a part-time degree in supply chain, probably two evenings a week for three years, and use AI at work to show what it can do. I'd ask Sandra to make me the person who tests new software. I'd also build up six months of savings by cutting about two hundred a month from takeaways and subscriptions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a long hill, not a wall. I'm anxious, but I know I can plan it, which makes sleep easier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With five years, how does your learning plan change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If firms waste that time I'd blame the owners, the private equity people who bought Lowfield. They will get the savings and call it efficiency, then wonder why nobody can afford their products. I'd want a law that makes them put some of the gain into the people they let go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does your blame go if firms use that time badly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first year I'd get the first two modules done and find out whether the degree really opens doors. If it doesn't, I'd switch to a trade-body certificate, which is shorter. I'm flexible about the route, as long as I don't just sit and wait.

say: I'd ask for a **retraining budget** for every buyer.
I'd say we should tax the profit and pay for it.
think: I'd have a **real choice** if I use AI hard for two years.
At 48 in 2031 I'd still have a long career.
do: Start a part-time **supply chain degree**, two evenings a week.
Become the person who tests new buying software at Lowfield.
Build six months of savings by cutting two hundred a month.
feel: A long hill, not a wall; sleeping is **easier** when I can plan.
S3.quote: I'd use AI hard for two years so that I'm the person who runs the new buying system, not the one it replaces.
fieldNote: Turns extra time into a **plan**: degree, savings and becoming the software tester.
Directs blame at the owners who capture the savings, not at technology.

steps.text: Start a part-time supply chain degree two evenings a week
Volunteer to test new buying software at Lowfield
Cut two hundred a month from takeaways and subscriptions
Back a law making firms share gains with laid-off staff

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's good to know early so we can plan properly. At work I'd just carry on and share what I learn about the tools. I'd also say to anyone listening that a decade is not an excuse to wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd feel fairly relaxed about my own job and more concerned about the kids. By 2036 Elin will be twenty and Jonas seventeen, choosing what to study, and I'd have no idea what to tell them. I'd stay uneasy rather than scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and keep building skills in small steps. Over ten years I'd finish a degree, keep paying down the mortgage so it's nearly gone by 2036, and maybe move into a technical sales role. I'd also push the union to bargain over AI now, because it's easier to agree rules early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels manageable, a bit like retirement planning. I'm not calm, since I know decades pass fast, but I'm not frightened either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is long. What would worry you about a long runway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A long runway makes people lazy, me included. If I think I've got ten years I'll put the course off until next year, then the year after. So I'd write down dates and ask Carla to hold me to them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you had to pick one thing to do now, what would it be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The one thing: sign up for the first evening class by January and pay the mortgage down quicker. If I only did one, I'd do the mortgage, because a smaller bill gives me more choices later.

say: I'd say a decade is **no excuse** to wait.
I'd share what I learn about the tools with colleagues.
think: I'm fairly relaxed about my own job and more concerned about **Elin and Jonas** choosing what to study.
I'd be uneasy rather than scared.
do: Finish a **degree** in small steps over ten years.
Pay the mortgage down so it's nearly gone by 2036.
Push the union to bargain over AI now.
feel: Manageable, like **retirement planning**, not calm but not frightened.
S4.quote: A long runway makes people lazy, me included. If I think I've got ten years I'll put the course off until next year, then the year after.
fieldNote: Worries he will **procrastinate** with a long runway; asks his partner to hold him to dates.
Thinks mostly about what to tell his children about study choices.

steps.text: Book the first evening class by January
Overpay the mortgage so it's nearly gone by 2036
Ask the union to bargain over AI rules early
Talk with Elin and Jonas about what to study

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. It's the only one where I lose the right to choose, and Carla's wage has to carry a family of four. What would help is notice periods in law, funded retraining that pays while you learn, and employers who say plainly what they plan to replace.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether I'd actually trust the tools, and I'd say only partly. I use them, I check everything, and I'd rather be the person who knows when the machine is wrong than the person who just reads out what it says.

headlineQuote: I'd rather be the person who knows when the machine is wrong than the person who just reads out what it says.
portrait: Ben, 43, is a **junior buyer** of fixings at Lowfield Building Supplies, with a nurse partner, two children and a mortgage.
He uses AI tools now and then and is pragmatic, but expects owners and new management to take the gains.
He leans on union action, regulation and his partner's secure ward job while he plans a part-time degree.
He moves from uneasy in mild worlds to alarmed only when AGI arrives in two years.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture worries him most, because it takes away his choices and leaves one wage.
whatWouldHelp: **Notice periods** in law, paid retraining and employers who say plainly what they plan to replace.
